title: Katherine Johnson: Calculating the Path to Space
summary: How Katherine Johnson used her gift for math to calculate the flight paths that sent American astronauts safely into orbit and back home.
poll: Careful, patient work behind the scenes can be just as important as the big moment everyone sees.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson Does the Math
versions.text:
As a girl, Katherine Johnson loved to count. She counted stars. She counted steps. She counted plates on the table. Numbers made sense to her. She liked them a lot. She was good at math.

Katherine was very smart at math. She finished school at 14. Then she went to college. Not many girls got to go then. Katherine did not stop. She kept on going.

She grew up. She got a job. Her job was math for a rocket team. She was a mathematician. All day, the team would calculate numbers by hand. It was hard work. But she liked it.

She worked hard. She wanted to do more. Men went to the big talks, but women did not. She kept asking to go. At last, she got to go, too.

She helped send the first man up to space in a rocket. She did the math for his trip. Later, John flew around Earth. A machine did the math first. But John wanted her to check it by hand.

Her math kept the men safe in space. Years later, she got a big prize. A film told her story, too. She showed the world what she could do.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson Does the Math
versions.text:
As a young girl, Katherine Johnson loved to count things. She counted the stars at night. She counted her steps to church. She counted the plates on the table. Numbers always made good sense to her.

Katherine was very smart at math. She finished high school at just 14. Then she went on to college. In those days, not many girls got that chance. Katherine did not stop.

Katherine took a job with a rocket team that sent men into space. She joined a team of women. They did hard math by hand. She was a mathematician. All day, she would calculate numbers for the team. It was hard, good work.

She worked hard and wanted to do more. At first, only men could go to the big talks. She kept on asking. At last, she was let in, too. Her ideas helped the team a lot.

She did the math that sent the first man up in a rocket. Later, John flew all the way around Earth. A machine checked the math first. But John wanted her to check it by hand.

Her careful math helped keep many men safe. Years later, she got a big prize. A movie told the story of her life. She showed the whole world what one mathematician could do.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson: Calculating the Path to Space
versions.text:
When Katherine Johnson was a young girl, she loved to count things. She counted the stars at night. She counted her steps. She counted the plates on the table. Numbers made more sense to her than almost anything else.

She grew up in a small town. She was very smart at math, even as a child. Few girls got the chance to study math back then. But she did not give up. She finished high school at only 14.

She went to college soon after. She studied hard and did well. Later, she got a job with a team that did math for rockets. Her job was to calculate numbers by hand.

She worked with that team for years. At first, only men could go to the big talks. She kept asking anyway. At last, she was let in, and her math helped the whole team.

In 1961, she did the math that sent the first man into space. A year later, John planned to fly all the way around Earth. A machine checked the math first, but John wanted her to check it by hand.

Her careful math helped keep many men safe. Years later, she got a big prize. A movie told the story of her life, showing what one mathematician could do.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson: Calculating the Path to Space
versions.text:
When Katherine Johnson was a young girl, she had a big love. She loved to count things. At night, she looked at the stars and counted them one by one.

Katherine grew up in a small town in West Virginia. She loved numbers and puzzles, and she loved school. In those days, very few girls, and very few Black girls, were given a chance to study hard math. Some people did not think Katherine could become a mathematician. But she did not give up on her love of numbers.

Katherine started college when she was only 14 years old. First, she studied hard math and other subjects. Later, she worked as a teacher for a few years. As a teacher, she helped many students learn their own math. She did this work for quite a while.

Then Katherine joined a team of women who did math for NASA. They would calculate the paths that rockets would take. Many people worked there, but few got picked for the hardest jobs. Katherine was one of them!

In 1961, Katherine worked out the path for the first American man to fly into space. She became known for her careful work. She spent years checking numbers by hand. Her math helped make sure each rocket's path was safe.

Today, people still tell young people about Katherine. She shows them that hard work with numbers can carry a person far in life.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson: Calculating the Path to Space
versions.text:
When Katherine Johnson was a young girl, she loved to count things. She counted the stars at night and hoped to understand them one day.

Katherine was born in 1918 and grew up in West Virginia, where strict segregation shaped daily life for Black families. She loved numbers and school work, and she was unusually quick at math. Her teachers noticed her gift early on. Very few women, and very few Black Americans, worked as scientists back then. Some people doubted that Katherine could become one. But she did not give up.

Katherine went to college when she was only 14. She studied math and French, two subjects she loved. Later, she worked for years as a schoolteacher. Then she took a job with a team of Black women known as human computers, since they did hard math by hand for NASA.

Katherine's job was to calculate the trajectory, or path, a rocket would follow through the sky. For a long time, only men could join the planning talks. Katherine kept asking, and at last she was let in.

In 1962, astronaut John Glenn flew a mission to orbit Earth. A new computer had already checked the math, but Glenn wanted Katherine to verify every number by hand before he agreed to fly.

Today, people still study Katherine's work. She shows them that careful numbers can carry a person far in life.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson: Calculating the Path to Space
versions.text:
When Katherine Johnson was a young girl, she had a deep love of numbers, and at night she gazed at the stars and dreamed of understanding how they moved across the sky above her small West Virginia town.

Katherine was born in 1918 and grew up in a place where strict segregation shaped daily life for Black families. Her teachers quickly noticed her gift for math, skipping her ahead several grades. Very few women and very few Black Americans worked as mathematicians in that era, and some people doubted that Katherine could ever succeed. However, her determination never weakened, even when doors seemed closed to her.

Katherine entered college at only 14 and earned top honors in both math and French. Afterward, she worked for several years as a schoolteacher. She then joined a group of Black women known as human computers, since they performed precision math by hand for NASA's engineers.

Katherine's job became calculating the trajectory, the exact path a rocket would follow through the sky. Solving the equations behind that path demanded total precision, since a single small mistake could be genuinely dangerous for the crew aboard.

In 1962, astronaut John Glenn prepared to orbit Earth aboard his spacecraft, becoming a true pioneer of American spaceflight. A computer had already checked the needed equations, but Glenn insisted that Katherine verify every figure by hand before he would agree to fly, trusting her accuracy completely.

In 1969, Katherine helped with calculations for the Moon landing, and in 1970 she helped bring the troubled Apollo 13 crew safely home after a dangerous emergency in space.

Katherine's journey shows that a barrier can be broken through patience and skill. Today, her legacy encourages young people, especially girls, to study math, and it reminds them that careful work can make even the boldest dream come true.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson: Calculating the Path to Space
versions.text:
As a young girl gazing nightly at the stars scattered across the sky above her small West Virginia town, Katherine Johnson held an unusually deep love of numbers, counting everything within sight and dreaming of someday understanding exactly how the stars themselves moved through the darkness overhead.

Born in 1918, Katherine was raised in a place where strict segregation shaped nearly every part of daily life for Black families, limiting the opportunities available to them in school, at work, and in countless ordinary public places throughout the region. Her teachers quickly recognized her unusual gift for mathematics and skipped her ahead several grades. At that time, very few women and an even smaller share of Black Americans worked as mathematicians, and skeptics often doubted whether Katherine could really overcome such steep barriers; even so, her determination never wavered despite considerable social doubt surrounding her ambitions.

Entering college at only fourteen years of age, Katherine earned top honors in both mathematics and French. She later worked for several years as a schoolteacher before joining a group of Black women mathematicians known as human computers, since they performed precise calculations entirely by hand for NASA's engineers, long before electronic machines existed to assist them in their daily labor.

Katherine's central responsibility became calculating the trajectory, the exact path a rocket would follow through the sky toward orbit. Solving the underlying equations demanded absolute precision, since even a single small error could prove genuinely dangerous for the crew riding aboard the fragile spacecraft.

By 1962, astronaut John Glenn was preparing to orbit Earth aboard his spacecraft, an achievement that would establish him as a true pioneer of American spaceflight. A newly installed electronic computer had already checked the necessary equations, yet Glenn insisted that Katherine personally verify every single figure by hand, trusting her precision completely over the still-untested machine.

In 1969, Katherine's calculations supported the Apollo 11 Moon landing, and in 1970 she helped bring the endangered Apollo 13 crew safely back home following a dangerous onboard emergency that threatened all of their lives deep in space, far from any possible rescue or any outside help of any kind whatsoever.

Katherine's remarkable path clearly shows that seemingly immense barriers can indeed be overcome through steady persistence and quiet, disciplined skill. Today, her enduring legacy encourages young people, particularly girls, to pursue mathematics, often demonstrating that curiosity combined with steady dedication can make even the boldest dream come true.

versions.title: Katherine Johnson: Calculating the Path to Space
versions.text:
As a young girl gazing nightly toward the stars scattered across the sky above her small West Virginia town, Katherine Johnson harbored an extraordinarily persistent love of numbers, counting virtually everything within sight and dreaming of someday comprehending exactly how the stars themselves moved through the surrounding darkness overhead.

Born in 1918, Katherine was raised in a place where rigid, systemic segregation shaped nearly every conceivable aspect of daily life for Black families, severely limiting the opportunities available to them in educational institutions, in employment, and in countless ordinary public places throughout the region. Her teachers quickly recognized her extraordinary aptitude for mathematics and repeatedly skipped her ahead through several grade levels. During that particular historical period, remarkably few women and an even smaller proportion of Black Americans occupied recognized positions as professional mathematicians, and persistent skeptics frequently doubted whether Katherine could realistically overcome such formidable institutional barriers; nevertheless, her determination remained fundamentally unshaken despite considerable societal discouragement surrounding her ambitions.

Matriculating at college when merely fourteen years of age, Katherine earned exceptionally high honors in both mathematics and French. She subsequently worked for several years as a schoolteacher before ultimately joining a specialized group of Black women mathematicians known collectively as human computers, since they performed intricate, precise calculations entirely by hand for NASA's engineering teams, long before electronic calculating machines existed to assist them in their demanding daily labor.

Katherine's central professional responsibility became calculating the trajectory, the exact mathematical path a rocket would follow through the sky toward sustained orbit. Solving the underlying equations governing that path demanded absolute, unwavering precision, since even a single comparatively small arithmetic error could prove genuinely catastrophic for the crew riding aboard the fragile spacecraft.

By 1962, astronaut John Glenn was actively preparing to orbit Earth aboard his spacecraft, an achievement that would ultimately establish him as a genuine pioneer of American spaceflight. A newly installed electronic computer had already independently verified the necessary equations, yet Glenn nonetheless insisted that Katherine personally verify every single figure by hand herself, trusting her mathematical precision considerably more than the still-untested electronic machine.

In 1969, Katherine's meticulous calculations directly supported the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, and in 1970 she subsequently helped bring the gravely endangered Apollo 13 crew safely back home following a dangerous onboard mechanical emergency that seriously threatened all of their lives deep within space, far removed from any possible outside rescue whatsoever.

Katherine's remarkable professional trajectory clearly demonstrates that seemingly immense, deeply entrenched barriers can indeed be overcome through steady, unwavering persistence and quiet, thoroughly disciplined skill. Today, her enduring scientific legacy continues to encourage young people, particularly girls from underrepresented backgrounds, to pursue demanding careers in mathematics, consistently demonstrating that intellectual curiosity combined with steady, lifelong dedication can render even the most audacious, boldest dream genuinely achievable.

LOW.prompt: Katherine Johnson kept asking until she was allowed to join the big talks. Write about a time you kept trying at something, like Katherine did.

I told what I did to keep trying, like Katherine did.
I used at least two key words, such as calculate or team.
LOW.modelAnswer: Last year, I kept trying to learn how to calculate fractions in math class. At first, I got the wrong answer many times, but I did not give up, just like Katherine Johnson did not give up when she asked to join the big talks. HIGH.prompt: Katherine Johnson is often called a pioneer. Explain what makes someone a pioneer and why Katherine fits that description, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what a pioneer is.

HIGH.modelAnswer: A pioneer is someone who breaks through barriers to accomplish something few or no people like them had done before, opening the way for others to follow. Katherine Johnson fits this description because she worked as a Black woman mathematician at NASA during an era of strict segregation, when very few people who looked like her were given such opportunities. Her precision was so trusted that astronaut John Glenn insisted she personally verify the equations behind his orbital trajectory by hand before he would agree to fly, even after an electronic computer had already checked the math. This evidence shows that Katherine's legacy as a pioneer rests on both her mathematical skill and her refusal to accept the barriers placed in her path.
